The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

articles.title_original: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
articles.excerpt_original: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

articles.title_original: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
articles.excerpt_original: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

articles.title_original: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
articles.excerpt_original: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

articles.title_original: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
articles.excerpt_original: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
